payload.claim: The authors hedge their interpretations throughout ('may underlie', 'might be associated', 'may reflect') and refuse to overclaim causal or clinical significance from cross-sectional correlational fMRI findings.

In the discussion they explicitly question whether the observed abnormalities reflect pathophysiology or dynamic disease progression and concede they cannot exclude antipsychotic-medication confounds.

They state a null finding plainly (no significant PANSS–VMHC associations in either frequency band) and devote a candid limitations passage to unavailable medication dosage data, limited statistical power, and the cross-sectional design.

Authors volunteer that 'none of the studies was designed to investigate metaphor,' flag that participants were U.S.-based and Harry-Potter-fluent, and disclose Google funding and an FTC affiliation — conduct that openly surfaces what undercuts the clean account.

The provocation explicitly declines the strong claim ('does not argue that some metaphors are good and others bad'), labels the synthesis 'interpretive,' and calls for future studies to 'test the empirical claims raised here' — calibrated, non-overclaiming stance.

Case 4 deliberately complicates the authors' own positive account by showing the praised metaphor mechanism becoming 'a tool for extracting disclosure' — turning a critical eye on their own argument rather than hiding its downside.

The discussion frames metaphor choice as an ethical decision and foregrounds how a framing 'hides institutional actors, data movement, and power asymmetries,' centering whom a design serves and what it conceals from young users.

The authors take an explicitly 'mostly unsettled' question and discharge it with full proofs (Theorems 1–4 plus a multi-section appendix), treating the matter as not closed until rigorously established.

They pair every upper bound with a matching minimax lower bound to prove near-optimality across the full range of the uncertainty level, and precisely quantify the factor by which prior upper/lower bounds were loose — a refusal to settle for one-sided guarantees.

The central claim is deliberately conditional — robustness is neither uniformly easier nor harder than standard RL; the verdict is indexed to the divergence metric and the size/shape of the uncertainty set rather than overgeneralized.

The authors state plainly where their own theory is tight (sigma of order one) and where it remains loose (by a polynomial horizon factor), disclosing the boundary of their contribution instead of obscuring it.

The authors cross-validate their novel ML-classifier sensitivity against the standard likelihood-ratio test as a benchmark, and re-test the result under alternative energy binnings, magnetic-field parameters, and EBL models (Appendix D), treating agreement as something to be earned.

The authors volunteer that their hyperparameter choice is 'somewhat arbitrary', that Asimov datasets 'cannot be reliably used' with their method, and that higher-confidence (3σ/5σ) limits 'should be regarded as less reliable' — disclosing weaknesses unprompted.

Spectral models are 'conservatively' extrapolated, results are framed as projected upper limits ('constraining ... rather than discovering'), and conclusions are consistently hedged, keeping claims calibrated to the simulated, model-dependent evidence.

The authors construct an explicit falsification criterion ('if signatures are absent, non-specific, or fully accounted for by these covariates... the dog-linked account is weakened or rejected'), plus negative controls, within-site contrasts, specificity tests, and competing explanations — all aimed at how their own hypothesis could fail.

The commentary's stance is heavily hedged and bounded ('may have contributed', 'biologically plausible and testable', 'currently untested in deep-time'), and repeatedly refuses to overclaim ('we do not claim genetic canalization', 'any contribution to genetic evolution... remains speculative'), scaling each claim to the evidence.

The authors volunteer the limits of their own proposal — 'this approach comes with caveats' (tissue specificity, only early-development changes recoverable), 'residual confounding effects are inevitable', and 'effect sizes may be modest' — disclosing what qualifies their case rather than concealing it.
